# Your First Plot {#sec-plot}

Once your data is in R, one line of code turns it into a picture. This chapter covers exactly two plots — the two you will reach for constantly — using nothing beyond base R, no extra packages required.

We will use the same `diet_habits.csv` dataset from @sec-open-files:

```{r}
#| eval: TRUE
survey <- read.csv("data/diet_habits.csv")
head(survey)
```

## Plot 1 — a continuous variable: `hist()`

The `hist()` function is the fastest way to see the shape of a numeric column — how the values are distributed. Let's look at `bmi`.

```{r}
#| eval: TRUE
hist(survey$bmi,
     main = "Distribution of BMI",
     xlab = "BMI (kg/m²)",
     col = "#001D41")
```

The chart below illustrates the same idea: it redraws a histogram-shaped distribution with a different number of bins, the same way `hist()` would if you changed the `breaks` argument.

::: {.plot-box}
<div class="bins">
  <button data-bins="5">5 bins</button>
  <button class="active" data-bins="8">8 bins</button>
  <button data-bins="12">12 bins</button>
</div>
<svg id="histSvg" viewBox="0 0 560 240" style="width:100%; height:auto;"></svg>
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Reading a histogram
Each bar covers a range of BMI values; its height is how many participants fall in that range. A tall bar in the middle and short bars at the edges — like above — means most participants have a BMI near the average, with a few higher and lower.
:::

## Plot 2 — a categorical variable: `barplot()`

For a column like `diet_type`, there is no "distribution" to draw — instead, we count how many participants fall into each category. In base R this takes two steps: count with `table()`, then plot the result.

```{r}
#| eval: TRUE
diet_counts <- table(survey$diet_type)
diet_counts
```

```{r}
#| eval: TRUE
barplot(diet_counts,
        main = "Participants per diet type",
        xlab = "Diet type",
        ylab = "Number of participants",
        col = "#3E8E7E")
```

`table(survey$diet_type)` counts how many rows fall into each unique category first; `barplot()` then draws one bar per count. This two-step pattern — count, then plot — is worth remembering, since it's exactly what `hist()` does for you automatically with numbers.

## Saving your plot

Every plot you make in RStudio or Posit Cloud appears in the **Plots** pane.

![The Plots pane after running the barplot code above. Circled in red: the "Export" button, which saves the current plot as a PNG or PDF straight into your `output/` folder.](figures/07-plots-pane-export.png){#fig-plots-export}

::: {.callout-tip}
## Which plot do I use?
- One numeric column, and you want to see its shape → `hist()`
- One category column, and you want to see counts per group → `table()` + `barplot()`
:::
